issues.description: In Experiment 1, the mixed model includes only a random intercept for subjects but no random intercept for items (suffixes/nonwords). This violates the principle of crossed random effects in psycholinguistic research (Clark, 1973; Baayen et al., 2008). Without a random intercept for items, the model does not account for variability across stimuli, inflating Type I error rates. Given that only 20 suffixes were used and each appeared only twice per participant, item-level variance is a serious concern.
issues.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the mixed model specification is described as 'identical to those in Experiment 1,' which again includes only a random intercept for subjects and not for items (suffixes). With only 11 suffixes, item-level random effects are essential. Failure to include them means the results may be driven by idiosyncratic properties of specific suffixes rather than the general phenomenon of interest.
issues.quote: The analyses were otherwise identical to those in Experiment 1.

issues.description: In Experiment 3, six eye-movement measures are tested (skipping, first fixation duration, first run dwell time, go-past time, regressions-in, regressions-out) with no correction for multiple comparisons. With six tests at alpha=0.05, the familywise error rate is approximately 26%. The two significant effects (go-past time and regressions-out) could plausibly be false positives. This is especially concerning given that the authors state they had 'no concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected.'
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures.

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the number of words pre-target differed significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions (4.75 vs. 5.23, t(64)=2.07, p<0.05). This is a statistically significant confound that the authors acknowledge but do not adequately address. More words before the target in the incongruent condition means more contextual information has accumulated, which could independently drive the observed congruency effects on go-past times and regressions-out, since these are late measures sensitive to contextual integration.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the nonwords used in congruent and incongruent conditions are different items (different stems combined with the same suffix). This means that any differences in nonword-level properties (e.g., phonological neighbourhood, orthographic neighbourhood, pronounceability, length) between the two sets could confound the congruency effect. The authors do not report matching of the nonwords themselves across conditions on these properties.
issues.quote: Each of the 30 suffixes appeared with four different stems, twice in a congruent sentence context, and twice in an incongruent one.

issues.description: Experiment 1 uses 46 participants but only 20 suffixes (each appearing twice per participant per list, with participants seeing only 40 items). Experiment 2 uses only 29 participants and 11 suffixes. No power analysis is reported for any experiment. Given the small number of suffix items and the reliance on graded diagnosticity/specificity as continuous predictors, the studies may be severely underpowered to detect the graded effects, particularly at the item level.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London... Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London.

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the token-based specificity analysis reports a z-value of 0.60 with p<0.01, which is internally inconsistent. A z-value of 0.60 corresponds to p≈0.55, not p<0.01. This appears to be a typographical or computational error that undermines confidence in the reported statistics.
issues.quote: As predicted, the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the reported estimate and t-value for go-past time are inconsistent between the main results table and the text. The table reports B=43, t=3.76, while the text reports B=41, t=3.837. These discrepancies suggest either a reporting error or that different model specifications were used in different places.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)... Go-past time | 458 (129) | 507 (125) | 49 | 43 | t = 3.76 ***

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the regressions-out effect is reported as B=0.3, z=3.12, p<0.01 in the text, but the table reports B=0.25, z=2.65. These are inconsistent and suggest either different model runs or reporting errors. The discrepancy in z-values (3.12 vs. 2.65) is large enough to affect interpretation.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01)... Regressions-out | 0.14 (0.1) | 0.17 (0.1) | 0.03 | 0.25 | z = 2.65 **

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the authors multiply diagnosticity by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes before entering it as a continuous predictor. This ad hoc sign transformation is not standard practice and conflates the direction of the effect with the magnitude. The authors then run separate analyses to verify the effect is not due to the transformation, but this post-hoc verification does not fully resolve the concern about the validity of the combined analysis.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.description: All three experiments use nonwords rather than real words. While this controls for lexical familiarity, it introduces an artificial situation where participants must process novel letter strings. The generalizability of findings to real word reading is assumed but not demonstrated. The use of nonwords in eye-tracking (Experiment 3) is particularly unusual and may engage different processing strategies than natural reading.
issues.quote: Eighty experimental nonwords with suffix spellings diagnostic for adjectives (10 suffixes) or nouns (10 suffixes) were selected from Experiment 1.

issues.description: Experiment 1 uses an explicit metalinguistic judgment task (deciding if a nonword 'looks like' a noun or adjective), yet the authors claim in the General Discussion that participants showed sensitivity 'without explicit instruction.' The task is inherently explicit and metacognitive, making it inappropriate to draw conclusions about implicit statistical learning from this experiment alone.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so (see our spelling and eye tracking data)

issues.description: Experiment 1 was conducted 'at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.' This introduces potential fatigue effects and means participants' performance may not reflect their typical processing. The nature of the prior testing session is not described, raising the possibility that it could have primed morphological or lexical category awareness.
issues.quote: This experiment was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.

issues.description: In Experiment 2, each participant saw all 66 sentences (within-subjects design), but the assignment of stems to congruent/incongruent conditions is not counterbalanced across participants. The same stem always appears in the same context type. This means that any stem-specific properties could systematically bias the congruent or incongruent condition.
issues.quote: Each participant heard six nonwords containing each suffix: three times in a context congruent with the target spelling of the suffix, and three times in a context incongruent with it.

issues.description: The diagnosticity measure is defined as the proportion of words with a given suffix that belong to a particular category. However, this is computed over the CELEX database which has known biases (e.g., overrepresentation of certain registers, underrepresentation of low-frequency words). The authors do not discuss how database composition might affect their diagnosticity and specificity estimates, or whether results would differ with a more balanced or contemporary corpus.
issues.quote: We extracted all single-word entries from the CELEX database (Baayen, Piepenbrock & van Rijn, 1993), excluding any entries with spaces or hyphens.

issues.description: The specificity measure requires identifying 'the most frequent pronunciation of each suffix.' However, many suffixes have multiple pronunciations (e.g., -ED is pronounced /t/, /d/, or /ɪd/), and using only the most frequent pronunciation may misclassify words and distort specificity estimates. The authors acknowledge using CELEX surface forms but do not discuss the impact of allophonic/allomorphic variation on their measures.
issues.quote: In order to calculate specificity, we identified the most frequent pronunciation of each suffix, and then extracted all words from our single-word database containing that word-final sound sequence.

issues.description: The inclusion of pseudoaffixed words (e.g., 'corner' for -ER) in the computation of diagnosticity and specificity is theoretically problematic. The authors justify this by citing evidence that people identify morphemes within pseudoaffixed words, but this conflates the linguistic reality of morpheme boundaries with readers' processing heuristics. Including pseudoaffixed words in the denominator of diagnosticity calculations could artificially inflate or deflate estimates.
issues.quote: We included pseudoaffixed words because there is evidence that people identify morphemes within these (Rastle, Davis, & New, 2004).

issues.description: The correlation between diagnosticity and specificity (r=0.53, p<0.0001) is used to argue that the two constructs are 'related although they capture distinct properties.' However, a correlation of 0.53 means the two measures share ~28% of variance, which could indicate substantial overlap rather than distinctiveness. The authors do not conduct a formal test of discriminant validity or demonstrate that both measures independently predict behavior.
issues.quote: The correlation between the type variables is 0.53, p < 0.0001; that between the token variables – 0.47, p < 0.0001. This indicates that the two constructs are related although they capture distinct properties of suffixes.

issues.description: The authors note that 'a substantial number of suffixes have diagnosticity and specificity values of 1,' and that mean type diagnosticity is 0.78 and mean specificity is 0.82. These high means with many values at ceiling suggest the distributions are heavily skewed. Using means and correlations on such distributions is problematic, and the authors do not report distributional statistics (skewness, kurtosis) or use appropriate non-parametric alternatives.
issues.quote: It is immediately apparent that a substantial number of suffixes have diagnosticity and specificity values of 1... Mean type diagnosticity for suffixes is 0.78 (token – 0.77), mean specificity is 0.82 (token – 0.83).

issues.description: The entropy analysis comparing spelling and phonology uses a regression slope test (slope=0.9, SE=0.04) to argue that spelling is more predictive of lexical category than phonology. However, the difference between the mean entropy values is trivially small (H_spelling=0.61 vs H_sound=0.63), and the practical significance of a slope of 0.9 vs. 1.0 is not discussed. The statistical significance of this difference does not imply meaningful practical difference.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01). That is, the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category (mean H=0.61) than do their spoken realisations (mean H=0.63).

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the main effect of suffix condition is reported (B=-1.57, z=-4.224, p<0.0001) but no measure of effect size is provided. Similarly, no effect sizes are reported for any of the three experiments. Without effect sizes, it is impossible to assess the practical significance of the findings or to use them for future power analyses.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses (B = -1.57, z = -4.224, p < 0.0001) than "adjective" responses.

issues.description: For Experiment 3, the authors state that 'all models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes' but do not report the full model specification including random slopes. In mixed models, the inclusion or exclusion of random slopes can substantially affect fixed effect estimates and their significance. The rationale for not including random slopes is not provided.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes. However, in the interest of space we report only those effects pertaining to our main variable of interest, congruency.

issues.description: The comprehension accuracy in Experiment 3 is reported as '0.86%' which is clearly a formatting error—it should be 86% (0.86 as a proportion). This type of error, while likely typographical, undermines confidence in the accuracy of other reported statistics.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the sentence contexts were designed to bias lexical category interpretation, but no norming data are provided to confirm that the contexts successfully and unambiguously conveyed the intended lexical category. Without norming, it is unclear whether the incongruent condition truly created a mismatch or whether some sentences were ambiguous.
issues.quote: Sixty-six sentences were designed following one of three possible context templates (noun, adjective, or verb template; see Table 4 for an example of each template).

issues.description: In Experiment 3, comprehension questions tested retention of nonwords on 50% of trials, but no data are reported on performance for the different question types (pre-target, post-target, nonword retention). This makes it impossible to assess whether participants were actually reading for comprehension or whether the comprehension check was effective.
issues.quote: Single comprehension questions (forced-choice yes/no answer) were presented immediately after the relevant sentence on 50% of trials to ensure engagement with the task. One third of these questions referred to the pre-target context... one-third – to the post-target context... one-third was the testing the retention of the nonwords.

issues.description: All participants were undergraduate students at a single UK university, limiting generalizability. More importantly, the authors make broad claims about 'skilled readers' and 'the average reader' without considering individual differences in reading ability, morphological awareness, or vocabulary size, which are known to moderate morphological processing effects.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so

issues.description: The authors argue that 'English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.' This is a strong evolutionary/functional claim that goes well beyond what the correlational computational analysis and behavioral experiments can support. The data show that regularities exist and influence behavior, but cannot establish that spelling-sound inconsistency evolved to maximize meaning transmission.
issues.quote: We close by arguing that English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.

issues.description: The authors do not adequately consider the alternative explanation that the observed behavioral effects in Experiments 1-3 are driven by low-level orthographic regularities (e.g., bigram frequencies, positional letter frequencies) rather than morphological knowledge per se. The authors discuss this briefly in the 'A note on orthography and morphology' section but do not include orthographic control conditions in any experiment.
issues.quote: Our view is that there are fundamental differences between low-level orthographic and morphological cues, in terms of the degree of precision with which the latter are encoded in written language

issues.description: None of the three experiments includes a condition with suffixes that have low diagnosticity/specificity as a baseline. Without such a control, it is impossible to determine whether the effects observed are due to high diagnosticity/specificity or simply to the presence of any suffix. The graded analyses partially address this, but a proper control condition would strengthen the design.
issues.quote: Twenty suffixes diagnostic for the noun or adjective category were selected (See Table 2). These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50

issues.description: In Experiment 1, 11.7% of data points were excluded due to timeouts or invalid button presses. This is a substantial exclusion rate for a simple two-alternative forced-choice task with a 2-second timeout. The authors do not analyze whether exclusions were systematic across conditions or suffix types, which could bias the results.
issues.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.description: In Experiment 1, suffixes were selected with diagnosticity ≥0.50, but this threshold is arbitrary and means that suffixes with diagnosticity just above 0.50 are included alongside those with diagnosticity of 1.0. The wide range of diagnosticity values within the selected set (e.g., -AN with 0.50 vs. -NESS with 1.00) makes the 'high diagnosticity' characterization of the stimulus set misleading.
issues.quote: These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50, and occurred in at least 20 different words.

issues.description: In Experiment 3, verb-suffix fillers were included but not analyzed because 'the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).' However, this means the filler items are systematically different from experimental items in their diagnosticity, potentially creating an asymmetry in the reading experience that could influence processing of the experimental items.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).

issues.description: The computational analysis excludes suffixes occurring in fewer than 20 words for some analyses but not others, and the rationale for this threshold is not clearly justified. Furthermore, the paper reports that 64 suffixes were excluded (leaving 95 of 154), but the main analyses appear to use all 154 suffixes. The relationship between the full and reduced analyses is not clearly articulated.
issues.quote: In order to determine this, we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged

issues.description: The paper does not report the viewing distance in degrees of visual angle for the nonword stimuli in Experiment 3, making it impossible to assess whether the eye-tracking setup was appropriate for detecting word-level effects. The character width is given (0.3°) but the total nonword length in degrees is not reported, which is critical for evaluating whether the interest area definitions were appropriate.
issues.quote: Participants were seated at a viewing distance of 140cm... All sentences were displayed in black Courier font (size 14pt, horizontal character width 0.3o)

issues.description: The paper frames diagnosticity as analogous to 'cue validity' and specificity as analogous to 'probability of a cue given a category,' which are the two conditional probabilities in Bayes' theorem. However, the authors do not engage with the extensive literature on cue validity and cue diagnosticity in categorization research (e.g., Rosch, 1978; Murphy & Medin, 1985), which would provide a richer theoretical framework and allow comparison with existing findings.
issues.quote: Diagnosticity on its own is reminiscent of what is referred to as cue validity (conditional probability of a category given a cue; Beach, 1964).

issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants were forced to choose between 'noun' and 'adjective' only, even though some suffixes in the stimulus set (e.g., -ER, -AN) are associated with multiple categories including verbs. This binary forced-choice format may artificially inflate apparent sensitivity to the noun-adjective distinction by eliminating the possibility of 'verb' or 'other' responses.
issues.quote: Participants indicated their adjective-noun decisions via button press.

issues.description: In Experiment 2, nonwords were recorded by a single female native speaker of British English. The use of a single speaker limits generalizability and introduces potential speaker-specific prosodic or phonetic cues that could influence spelling decisions independently of the intended phonological sequence. No information is provided about whether the recordings were checked for consistency or whether any items were re-recorded.
issues.quote: The nonwords were pronounced by an adult female native speaker of British English and recorded in stereo at a sampling rate of 22,050 Hz.

issues.description: The authors report a convergence warning for the regressions-out model in Experiment 3 and address it by refitting with a different optimizer. While the approach (comparing fits across optimizers) is reasonable, the authors do not report whether the original model's parameter estimates were trustworthy or whether the warning indicated a genuine estimation problem. The decision to report only the refitted model without the original estimates makes it impossible to assess the robustness of the solution.
issues.quote: The original model produced a convergence warning when the variables were added. One way to assess if this warning is a false positive is to refit this model using a different optimisation procedure, such as "bobyqa" (Powell, 2009). We did this, and observed that the fits of these two models and the significance levels for the fixed effects were identical

issues.description: The authors claim that 'diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.' This is a strong universalist claim made without any supporting data from other languages. The authors acknowledge this is conjecture but present it as a conclusion rather than a hypothesis.
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.description: The paper does not report the inter-rater reliability for the manual extraction of suffix spellings from whole nonword spellings in Experiment 2. Given that this is a subjective coding process (deciding where the suffix begins in a participant's spelling), the reliability of this coding is critical to the validity of the dependent variable.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings (1,914 analysable data points).

issues.description: The paper focuses on three lexical categories (noun, adjective, verb) but many English words are genuinely ambiguous across categories (e.g., 'play' as noun or verb). The authors create separate entries for such words in CELEX, but this means that the same word contributes to the diagnosticity/specificity calculations for multiple categories, potentially inflating ambiguity estimates and deflating diagnosticity values for suffixes that appear in genuinely ambiguous words.
issues.quote: Separate entries were created for words that could express different lexical categories (e.g. PLAY as a noun or as a verb).

issues.description: The computational analysis and all experiments focus on nouns, adjectives, and verbs, but exclude adverbs. The suffix -LY is the most frequent suffix in the dataset (type frequency 2717) and is strongly associated with adverbs (diagnosticity for adverbs would be very high). By excluding adverbs, the authors may be misclassifying -LY words and distorting the diagnosticity/specificity estimates for other categories. The -LY suffix appears in Appendix A with near-zero diagnosticity for all three categories, which is anomalous.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs.

issues.description: The paper does not report whether participants in Experiments 1, 2, and 3 were the same individuals or different groups. Given that all experiments were conducted at the same institution with the same participant pool (undergraduate students at Royal Holloway), there is a risk of participant overlap across experiments, which could introduce demand characteristics or practice effects.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London... Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London... 47 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway University of London were recruited following the same procedure as in Experiments 1 and 2.

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the authors use chi-square difference tests to assess whether adding diagnosticity and its interaction with congruency improves model fit. However, they do not report the degrees of freedom for these tests correctly—Chi(2) is reported but the number of parameters added is not clearly specified. Furthermore, model comparison using likelihood ratio tests requires models to be fit with maximum likelihood (ML) rather than restricted maximum likelihood (REML), and it is not stated which was used.
issues.quote: The fit of go-past model improved significantly when the interaction and the main effect of diagnosticity were added: Chi (2) = 8.58, p < 0.05.

issues.description: In Experiments 2 and 3, the sentence templates for different lexical categories are structurally different (e.g., noun contexts use 'direct/indirect object following an adjective,' adjective contexts use specific linking verbs, verb contexts use adverbs). These structural differences mean that the syntactic position and surrounding words differ systematically across conditions, confounding lexical category with syntactic structure and potentially with the predictability of the target position.
issues.quote: Nonwords in the noun context template occupied the syntactic position of a direct/indirect object following an adjective, and so could only be interpreted as nouns. Nonwords in adjective contexts appeared after verbs prove, stay, grow, smell, appear, taste, sound, seem, look, turn, become, remain
